blocks.content: Explore dashboards on Grafana Play to understand the intent of each panel and whether it fulfills that intent, where a panel's data comes from, and what its unit tells you.
Open **Grafana Dashboard**.
The dashboard's title, Grafana Dashboard, doesn't say what it's about. Its panel titles do: the memory and CPU one server uses, the people logging in, the requests it serves.
Find the **Memory / CPU** panel.
The title says exactly what the graph represents, and the values carry a unit, bytes, so the viewer doesn't have to think about it.
Notice the **server requests** panel.
Now focus on the **logins** panel.

Both the logins and server requests  panels show the server's traffic, and both titles tell you what the graph represents at a glance. Their values are plain counts with no unit suffix, which suits requests and logins.
View the first **Google hits** bar gauge.

Here's a vertical bar gauge with five bars labeled A-series to E-series. Nothing says what each bar measures. Its unit is percent on a fixed 0 to 100 range, but hits are a count, not a share of anything. So the label is misleading.
Now, notice the second **Google hits** bar gauge.

Here's the same five unnamed bars, this time with no unit, still on a fixed 0 to 100 range. The colors change at 40, 60, 70, and 80. But with no unit, the viewer can't tell what the color changes mean.
Next, look at the **Google hits** gauge.
This gauge suggests a value approaching a limit. The limit is 300 with no unit, and the single series is labeled A-series. Nothing on the panel says what 300 hits would mean.
Focus on the third **Google hits** bar gauge.
Here's a horizontal bar gauge with six bars named for servers, Backend-ops-01 to Frontend-web-02. The names help, but there is still no unit.

Four panels, one title, no descriptions. A viewer must figure out what each one represents and how they differ. That is cognitive load the dashboard adds instead of reducing.

A focused version would keep **Memory / CPU**, **Memory**, **server requests**, and **logins**, and drop the **Google hits** repeats.
Explore a panel to view the data it visualizes.

blocks.title: Find the query and its data source

blocks.content: Open **SQL Expressions Showcase**.
Find the **Base Query (A) - Total CPU Usage** panel.
Open the panel for editing.

steps.reftarget: div[data-viz-panel-key='panel-3'] button[data-testid='data-testid Panel menu Base Query (A) - Total CPU Usage']
steps.description: Click here to open the panel menu.
Click Edit to open the panel editor.

blocks.content: Notice the data source for query **A**. It's a Prometheus data source, so Grafana sends this query to Prometheus.
This is the query for the visualization.

Below the query, the options row shows **Format: Time series**. Format determines how the result is interpreted in the panel, so it must suit the visualization: the Table format, for example, works only in a table. A stat or gauge can still take a time series result by reducing it to one value.
Expand **Standard options** if it's collapsed.

blocks.reftarget: [data-testid='data-testid Standard options Unit field property editor']
blocks.content: Under **Standard options**, the panel's **Unit** is set to **core**, the unit its values are measured in.
Leave the editor.

steps.description: Click Back to return to the dashboard.

steps.reftarget: button[data-testid='data-testid Exit edit mode button'], button[data-testid='data-testid Edit dashboard button']
steps.description: The dashboard is still in edit mode. Click Exit edit.

blocks.content: If Grafana asks about unsaved changes, select **Discard**. Nothing needed saving.
Explore the Memory gauge.

blocks.title: Connect the setting to the label

blocks.content: Open **Grafana Dashboard**.
Find the **Memory** gauge and notice the B suffix beside its value.
Open the panel for editing.

steps.description: Click here to open the panel menu.
Click Edit to open the panel editor.

blocks.content: Expand **Standard options** if it's collapsed.

blocks.reftarget: [data-testid='data-testid Standard options Unit field property editor']
blocks.content: Find **Unit** and read its **bytes(IEC)** setting.

The **Memory** panel formats its numeric value as bytes. B means bytes. Larger values can use units such as KiB or MiB. Unit formatting changes the display, not the query's data, and doesn't change timestamps into byte values.

Switching the unit to percent wouldn't turn these byte values into a percentage of memory. The numbers would stay the same and be labeled incorrectly. The unit has to describe what the query returns.
Leave the editor.

steps.description: Click Back to return to the dashboard.

steps.reftarget: button[data-testid='data-testid Exit edit mode button'], button[data-testid='data-testid Edit dashboard button']
steps.description: The dashboard is still in edit mode. Click Exit edit.

blocks.content: If Grafana asks about unsaved changes, select **Discard**. Nothing needed saving.
Explore a dashboard to see which of its panels measure the machine's resources, the USE method, and which measure the service as its users experience it, the RED method.
Open **Sample Website Dashboard**.
Find the **Memory / CPU** panel.
Focus on the **Memory** gauge.
Both measure a machine's resources, so they belong to the USE method. Both show how much of the resource is in use: utilization.
Find the **server requests** panel.
Focus on the **client side full page load** panel.

Both measure the service as its users experience it, so they belong to the RED method. Requests over time is the rate. Page load time is the duration.

RED has a third measurement, errors. There is no panel that counts failing requests, so this dashboard can't tell you whether requests are failing.

The four golden signals name the same three service measurements as RED, as traffic, errors, and latency, and add saturation: how close a resource is to its capacity. No panel here shows that either.

The remaining panels, **logins**, **Google hits**, **Support calls**, and **Sign ups**, are business measurements. Neither method covers them. The methods tell you what a health dashboard needs, not what every dashboard must contain.
